newsitem.title: UK: Marketing key to success on Internet, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Marketing key to success on Internet, experts say.

text.p: The Internet offers vast commercial opportunities, but Websites must be well designed, promoted and marketed if they are to succeed, Internet experts say.
"There's a kind of 'build it and they will come' mentality to the Net," Natalie Angelillio, vice president of content development for PhotoDisc Inc., said at a recent advertising industry conference.

PhotoDisc, a U.S.-based digital stock photo house whose Web site (www.photodisc.com) debuted in late 1995, learned, however that a successful Website is the product of careful planning and execution. And the hardest work is not over when the Website goes live.
"The day you put a site up (on the Web) is not the end, it's a beginning," Angelillo said last week at London's "Creative Show".

PhotoDisc decided to establish a site on the Internet's World Wide Web after seeing the business opportunity afforded by marketing its compact disc-based photo business over the Internet. Because the company's products can be delivered as well as ordered via the Internet, marketing over the Web presented the opportunity to offer clients instant delivery, Angelillo said.

But Angelillo said that while PhotoDisc investment is paying off, developing and maintaining a Web site is not easy. PhotoDisc is now generating monthly revenues of about $250,000 off its Website and expects to generate about 50 percent of its total sales off the Web by 2000, she said.
"Our president likes to say we're on the bleeding edge of technology, and many days it's felt like that," she said.
The cost of creating a Website is often much higher than expected, and many UK companies remain reluctant to commit serious financial resources to their Internet projects.

Tony Martin, managing director for Music Network, a designer of Websites for music and entertainment companies, said that while U.S. companies are willing to spend $1.0 million developing a single Website, British companies will generally spend only a fraction of that amount.
The trend in Britain is, however, improving, Martin said.
"A while ago I'd be surprised to get 20, 30 grand out of a medium-sized (record) label," he said. "Now I'm starting to get that out of individual bands."
-- Leslie Adler, London Advertising Newsdesk +44 171 542 2815 leslie.adler@reuters.com
